svg.aria-label: The anatomy of a clinical trial as a flow: the population enrolled, randomization, the two arms, what the comparison arm actually received, blinding, the outcome measured, the follow up window and the difference reported, with the question a reader should ask at each point.

g.text: Every box below is a place where a trial can quietly answer a different question from the one you asked.
Each part of a trial is a place
where the design can answer a

g.data-tip: Ask who was let in and who was kept out. Most people with acute low back pain improve within weeks whatever is done, which is why any uncontrolled series in that population looks like a success, and why the enrolled population decides in advance how much room a treatment has to show anything at all.
g.text: who was let in, and who was not

g.data-tip: Ask whether allocation was concealed until the moment of assignment. Randomization is the only feature of a trial that balances the causes nobody thought to measure, and it does that job only if the person enrolling the next patient cannot see which arm is coming next.

Ask what dose. Reviews of spinal manipulation are graded low to very low certainty partly because technique, force, number of sessions and frequency differ from trial to trial, so the arm labeled manipulation is not the same intervention twice and a pooled result is an average over several different treatments.

This is the one that fools people. Ask what the control group actually received and whether you would expect it to do nothing at all. One Cochrane review of chronic low back pain reported a small improvement in pain against sham, a medium improvement against no treatment, and little to no difference against other conservative care. Same treatment, three verdicts, and the whole difference sits in the other arm.
g.text: one review, chronic low back pain

g.data-tip: Ask who was blinded and to what. Manual therapy has a particular problem here: nobody can be blinded to receiving a thrust, a sham convincing enough to fool the patient may not be inert, and one that is certainly inert is rarely convincing. The practitioner is never blinded at all, so at the very least ask whether the person recording the outcome was.
g.text: could either side tell which arm the patient was in?

g.data-tip: Ask who held the pencil. Manipulative therapy for infantile colic looked effective on unblinded parent reported crying time, a reduction of roughly one hour and twelve minutes a day, and the effect no longer reached statistical significance once the analysis was restricted to trials with blinded observers. A patient reported outcome in an unblinded trial measures the treatment and the expectation together.

Ask when it was measured and for how long. A meta analysis of manipulation for cervicogenic headache found small statistically significant short term improvements in pain intensity, pain frequency and disability, and no significant effect at intermediate or long term follow up. A treatment that works this week and not next month is a different offer from the one usually advertised.
g.text: measured when, and for how long?

g.data-tip: Ask whether the difference is one a patient would notice, which is a different question from whether it is statistically significant. Guideline reviewers described manipulation as producing minimal improvement in function against sham manipulation on low quality evidence, and a meta analysis of migraine reported a confidence interval running across zero in both directions, meaning the data are compatible with no effect at all.

g.text: No trial is refuted by its anatomy. The anatomy tells you which question the trial actually answered.
